claim: 1300 nm three-photon calcium imaging has emerged as a useful technique to allow calcium imaging in deep brain regions.
source: 1300 nm three-photon calcium imaging has emerged as a useful technique to allow calcium imaging in deep brain regions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general assertion about the technique.

claim: The minimum photon count required for detection of calcium transients in GCaMP6s-expressing neurons was calculated and experimentally verified for 920 nm two-photon and 1320 nm three-photon excitation.
source: We calculated and experimentally verified the excitation pulse energy to achieve the minimum photon count required for the detection of calcium transients in GCaMP6s-expressing neurons for 920 nm two-photon and 1320 nm three-photon excitation.
evidence: The abstract states this was both calculated and experimentally verified.

claim: The cross-over depth beyond which three-photon microscopy outperforms two-photon microscopy in recording fidelity was quantified by considering combined effects of in-focus signal attenuation and out-of-focus background generation.
source: By considering the combined effects of in-focus signal attenuation and out-of-focus background generation, we quantified the cross-over depth beyond which three-photon microscopy outpeforms two-photon microscopy in recording fidelity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this quantification was performed.

claim: Brain tissue heating by continuous three-photon imaging was simulated with Monte Carlo method.
source: Brain tissue heating by continuous three-photon imaging was simulated with Monte Carlo method and experimentally validated with immunohistochemistry.
evidence: The abstract states Monte Carlo simulation was used.

claim: Brain tissue heating by continuous three-photon imaging was experimentally validated with immunohistochemistry.
source: Brain tissue heating by continuous three-photon imaging was simulated with Monte Carlo method and experimentally validated with immunohistochemistry.
evidence: The abstract states immunohistochemistry was used for experimental validation.

claim: Increased immunoreactivity was observed with 150 mW excitation power at 1 mm imaging depth.
source: Increased immunoreactivity was observed with 150 mW excitation power at 1 and 1.2 mm imaging depths.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this observation.

claim: Increased immunoreactivity was observed with 150 mW excitation power at 1.2 mm imaging depth.
source: Increased immunoreactivity was observed with 150 mW excitation power at 1 and 1.2 mm imaging depths.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this observation.

claim: 2-photon microscopy has enabled activity recording from thousands of neurons with single-cell resolution in the mouse brain.
source: In the mouse brain, 2-photon microscopy (2PM) has enabled activity recording from thousands of neurons with single-cell resolution (Sofroniew et al., 2016; Stirman et al., 2016; Weisenburger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In 2-photon excitation, background intensity eventually becomes comparable to the signal in non-sparsely labeled samples as excitation power grows exponentially with imaging depth.
source: Although 2-photon excitation (2PE) can effectively reduce out-of-focus fluorescence, the background intensity eventually becomes comparable to the signal in non-sparsely labeled samples, as the excitation power grows exponentially with imaging depth.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of 2PE.

claim: Background in 2-photon microscopy reduces image contrast.
source: The background not only reduces image contrast but also introduces additional noise inseparable from the true calcium transient signal, which irreversibly reduces imaging quality.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of background fluorescence.

claim: Background in 2-photon microscopy introduces additional noise inseparable from the true calcium transient signal.
source: The background not only reduces image contrast but also introduces additional noise inseparable from the true calcium transient signal, which irreversibly reduces imaging quality.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of background fluorescence.

claim: In the mouse neocortex, 2PM signal-to-background ratio decreases to one at approximately 4.7 attenuation lengths with a labeling density of approximately 2%.
source: In the mouse neocortex, 2PM signal-to-background ration (SBR) decreases to one at ~4.7 attenuation lengths with a labeling density of ~2% (Kobat et al., 2011; Theer et al., 2003; Theer and Denk, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 3-photon microscopy has emerged as a useful tool for imaging in deep brain regions that are typically inaccessible to 2PM.
source: 3-photon microscopy (3PM) has emerged as a useful tool for imaging in deep brain regions that are typically inaccessible to 2PM.
evidence: This is stated as a general assertion about 3PM capabilities.

claim: Deep calcium imaging with 2PM using red-shifted calcium indicators at 1100 nm excitation suffers from limitations such as staining only a single layer of cortical neurons.
source: Although deep calcium imaging with 2PM has been demonstrated with red-shifted calcium indicators using 1100 nm excitation, these methods suffer from limitations such as staining only a single layer of the cortical neurons (Tischbirek et al., 2015), or in the hippocampus of young mice less than 6 weeks old (Inoue et al., 2019; Kondo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Deep calcium imaging with 2PM using red-shifted calcium indicators at 1100 nm excitation is limited to the hippocampus of young mice less than 6 weeks old.
source: Although deep calcium imaging with 2PM has been demonstrated with red-shifted calcium indicators using 1100 nm excitation, these methods suffer from limitations such as staining only a single layer of the cortical neurons (Tischbirek et al., 2015), or in the hippocampus of young mice less than 6 weeks old (Inoue et al., 2019; Kondo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The best red-shifted GECIs are currently less than 40% the cross section of GCaMP6s.
source: Furthermore, the best red-shifted GECIs are currently less bright and robust than their green counterparts (e.g.,<40% the cross section of GCaMP6s and <50% sensitivity of jGCaMP7; Dana et al., 2019; Dana et al., 2016), which further limits their application to large-scale recordings.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The best red-shifted GECIs have less than 50% sensitivity of jGCaMP7.
source: Furthermore, the best red-shifted GECIs are currently less bright and robust than their green counterparts (e.g.,<40% the cross section of GCaMP6s and <50% sensitivity of jGCaMP7; Dana et al., 2019; Dana et al., 2016), which further limits their application to large-scale recordings.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The shorter 2PE wavelength (900–960 nm) for GCaMP results in more tissue scattering compared to red GECIs.
source: Compared to the red GECIs, the shorter 2PE wavelength (900–960 nm) for GCaMP results in more tissue scattering (Jacques, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: 2-photon imaging with GCaMP usually requires the removal of the superficial cortex or the insertion of penetrating optical elements.
source: Consequently, 2-photon imaging with GCaMP faces more technical challenges in the deep brain, and usually requires the removal of the superficial cortex or the insertion of penetrating optical elements (Attardo et al., 2015; Dombeck et al., 2010; Low et al., 2014; Pilz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 1300 nm 3PM has enabled activity imaging with GCaMP6 of the entire densely labeled cortex.
source: In comparison, 1300 nm 3PM has enabled activity imaging with GCaMP6 of the entire densely labeled cortex (Takasaki et al., 2020; Yildirim et al., 2019) and the hippocampus in intact adult mouse brains (8–16 weeks old) (Ouzounov et al., 2017; Takasaki et al., 2020; Weisenburger et al., 2019) because of the background suppression by 3-photon excitation (3PE) and the reduced tissue attenuation by the longer excitation wavelength (Ouzounov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 1300 nm 3PM has enabled activity imaging with GCaMP6 of the hippocampus in intact adult mouse brains (8–16 weeks old).
source: In comparison, 1300 nm 3PM has enabled activity imaging with GCaMP6 of the entire densely labeled cortex (Takasaki et al., 2020; Yildirim et al., 2019) and the hippocampus in intact adult mouse brains (8–16 weeks old) (Ouzounov et al., 2017; Takasaki et al., 2020; Weisenburger et al., 2019) because of the background suppression by 3-photon excitation (3PE) and the reduced tissue attenuation by the longer excitation wavelength (Ouzounov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 1300 nm 3PM enables deep brain imaging because of background suppression by 3-photon excitation.
source: In comparison, 1300 nm 3PM has enabled activity imaging with GCaMP6 of the entire densely labeled cortex (Takasaki et al., 2020; Yildirim et al., 2019) and the hippocampus in intact adult mouse brains (8–16 weeks old) (Ouzounov et al., 2017; Takasaki et al., 2020; Weisenburger et al., 2019) because of the background suppression by 3-photon excitation (3PE) and the reduced tissue attenuation by the longer excitation wavelength (Ouzounov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 1300 nm 3PM enables deep brain imaging because of reduced tissue attenuation by the longer excitation wavelength.
source: In comparison, 1300 nm 3PM has enabled activity imaging with GCaMP6 of the entire densely labeled cortex (Takasaki et al., 2020; Yildirim et al., 2019) and the hippocampus in intact adult mouse brains (8–16 weeks old) (Ouzounov et al., 2017; Takasaki et al., 2020; Weisenburger et al., 2019) because of the background suppression by 3-photon excitation (3PE) and the reduced tissue attenuation by the longer excitation wavelength (Ouzounov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: High-quality calcium imaging enables reliable detection of calcium transients in the presence of noise.
source: High-quality calcium imaging enables reliable detection of calcium transients in the presence of noise.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle.

claim: The effective attenuation length at 1320 nm in the mouse cortex is 297 ± 11 μm.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, the effective attenuation length (EAL) at 1320 nm in the mouse cortex is almost twice of that at 920 nm (297 ± 11 μm vs. 153 ± 10 μm, mean ± standard deviation, n = 4, >12 weeks old mice, all males, Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The effective attenuation length at 920 nm in the mouse cortex is 153 ± 10 μm.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, the effective attenuation length (EAL) at 1320 nm in the mouse cortex is almost twice of that at 920 nm (297 ± 11 μm vs. 153 ± 10 μm, mean ± standard deviation, n = 4, >12 weeks old mice, all males, Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The effective attenuation length at 1320 nm is almost twice that at 920 nm in the mouse cortex.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, the effective attenuation length (EAL) at 1320 nm in the mouse cortex is almost twice of that at 920 nm (297 ± 11 μm vs. 153 ± 10 μm, mean ± standard deviation, n = 4, >12 weeks old mice, all males, Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At the brain surface, 3PE at 1320 nm requires about 15 times the pulse energy of 2PE at 920 nm to generate the same amount of signal in fluorescein-labeled blood vessels.
source: To generate the same amount of signal in fluorescein-labeled blood vessels located at the brain surface, 3PE requires about 15 times the pulse energy of 2PE (1.1 ± 0.03 nJ vs. 0.07 ± 0.004 nJ, mean ± 95% confidence interval).
evidence: This is measured experimentally.

claim: 3PE becomes more power-efficient than 2PE at a depth of around 750 μm (the cross-over depth) in fluorescein-labeled blood vessels.
source: Eventually, 3PE becomes more power-efficient than 2PE at a depth of around 750 μm, which is defined here as the cross-over depth.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data.

claim: At the brain surface, 3PE at 1320 nm requires approximately 8 times the pulse energy as 2PE at 920 nm for GCaMP6s-labeled neurons.
source: At the brain surface, 3PE at 1320 nm requires ~8 times the pulse energy as 2PE at 920 nm (1.86 ± 0.27 nJ vs. 0.24 ± 0.05 nJ, mean ± 95% confidence interval)
evidence: This is measured experimentally.

claim: In cortical layers at around 700 μm depth, the pulse energy required for 3PE becomes comparable to that of 2PE at the brain surface for GCaMP6s-labeled neurons.
source: while in cortical layers at the depth around 700 μm, the pulse energy required for 3PE becomes comparable to that of 2PE at the brain surface.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data.

claim: The measured ratio of 3PE to 2PE pulse energy and cross-over depth are in good agreement with calculation based on typical 2PE and 3PE cross sections.
source: The measured ratio of the 3PE to 2PE pulse energy and the cross-over depth are in good agreement with the calculation based on the typical value of 2PE and 3PE cross sections (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as agreement between measurement and calculation.

claim: With the same repetition rate and pulse duration, 3PM is more power-efficient than 2PM when imaging in the deep cortex and beyond.
source: Our data show that, with the same repetition rate and pulse duration, 3PM is more power-efficient than 2PM when imaging in the deep cortex and beyond.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data.

claim: At approximately 1 mm imaging depth, 2PM repetition rate would have to be reduced to the same level as 3PM (typically ~1 MHz) to avoid tissue heating by average power.
source: In other words, even if 2PM were used to image at the same depth (e.g.,~1 mm), its repetition rate will have to be reduced to the same level as 3PM (typically ~1 MHz) to avoid tissue heating by the average power.
evidence: This is inferred from the power efficiency comparison.

claim: Previous studies on deep brain 2-photon imaging reduced repetition rates to below 1 MHz at approximately 1 mm imaging depth.
source: This result is consistent with previous studies on deep brain 2-photon imaging, where the repetition rates were reduced to below 1 MHz at ~1 mm imaging depth (Theer et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: For both 2PM and 3PM, the background is negligible at the sample surface, with SBR approximately 100 in fluorescein-labeled blood vessels.
source: For both 2PM and 3PM, the background is negligible at the sample surface, with SBR ~100 in fluorescein-labeled blood vessels (Figure 2A and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: As imaging depth increases beyond 600 μm in the cortex, 920 nm 2PM background starts to increase rapidly.
source: As the imaging depth increases beyond 600 μm in the cortex, 920 nm 2PM background starts to increase rapidly, accompanied by apparent degradation of image quality (Figure 2A and Figure 2C lower panel).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claim: The fractional vascular volume in fluorescein-labeled blood vessels is 2 ± 1%.
source: Since the SBR of 2PM depends on the staining density of the sample, we quantified the fractional vascular volume (2 ± 1%, mean ± standard deviation) and staining inhomogeneity (~50) of the labeled blood vessels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 – Materials and methods).
evidence: This is measured experimentally.

claim: The staining inhomogeneity of fluorescein-labeled blood vessels is approximately 50.
source: Since the SBR of 2PM depends on the staining density of the sample, we quantified the fractional vascular volume (2 ± 1%, mean ± standard deviation) and staining inhomogeneity (~50) of the labeled blood vessels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 – Materials and methods).
evidence: This is measured experimentally.

claim: According to theoretical calculation, the SBR of 2PM reaches one at approximately 4.7 EALs at a staining inhomogeneity of 50.
source: According to the theoretical calculation, the SBR of 2PM reaches one at ~4.7 EALs at such a staining inhomogeneity (Theer and Denk, 2006), which is in close agreement with our in vivo measurement (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on theoretical calculation cited from previous work and agrees with experimental measurement.

claim: 1320 nm 3PM does not show any increase in background until in the white matter.
source: In contrast, 1320 nm 3PM does not show any increase in the background until in the white matter (Figure 2A and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Large SBRs (>40) were reported on 3-photon imaging of mouse brain vasculature at an imaging depth greater than 5 EALs.
source: Large SBRs (>40) were reported on 3-photon imaging of mouse brain vasculature at an imaging depth of greater than 5 EALs (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: For depths beyond the white matter, the measured SBR of 3PM is lower than theoretical prediction, possibly due to deterioration of the point spread function from strong aberration induced by white matter.
source: However, for the depths beyond the white matter, our measured SBR of 3PM is lower than the theoretical prediction, which may be caused by the deterioration of the point spread function due to the strong aberration induced by the white matter.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between measurement and theory.

claim: From neurons in shallow mouse cortical layer 2/3 and 4, nearly identical calcium traces were obtained with 2PM and 3PM.
source: From the neurons in the shallow mouse cortical layer 2/3 and 4, we obtained nearly identical calcium traces with 2PM and 3PM (Figure 2C upper panel), with a Pearson's correlation factor of 0.98 ± 0.01 (mean ± standard error, calculated from 60 traces, each 75 s from neurons located from 200 to 400 μm in depth).
evidence: This is measured experimentally and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Pearson's correlation factor between 2PM and 3PM calcium traces in shallow cortical layers is 0.98 ± 0.01.
source: From the neurons in the shallow mouse cortical layer 2/3 and 4, we obtained nearly identical calcium traces with 2PM and 3PM (Figure 2C upper panel), with a Pearson's correlation factor of 0.98 ± 0.01 (mean ± standard error, calculated from 60 traces, each 75 s from neurons located from 200 to 400 μm in depth).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: Similar results of ΔF/F deterioration in 2PM have been observed in other densely labeled transgenic lines (Slc17a7/ai162) by independent studies.
source: Similar results have been observed in other densely labeled transgenic lines (Slc17a7/ai162) by independent studies (Takasaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Laser-induced tissue damage can be categorized into thermal and nonlinear damage.
source: Laser-induced tissue damage can be categorized into thermal and nonlinear damage, with distinct mechanisms and dependence on imaging parameters.
evidence: This is stated as a general categorization.

claim: Continuous heating damages brain tissue through high temperature, which disturbs various biophysical processes.
source: Continuous heating damages the brain tissue through high temperature, which disturbs various biophysical processes (Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Heating-induced damage happens in the bulk tissue and depends on the average power per illumination volume.
source: Heating-induced damage happens in the bulk tissue and depends on the average power per illumination volume.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of thermal damage.

claim: Nonlinear damage is caused by the strong electric field at the focal point.
source: On the other hand, nonlinear damage is caused by the strong electric field at the focal point, which is related to focal spot size, pulse energy, and pulse duration.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of nonlinear damage.

claim: Brain tissue damage was observed at >250 mW average power of continuous 920 nm illumination in both anesthetized and awake mice with cranial windows.
source: The previous works showed that brain tissue damage was observed at >250 mW average power of continuous 920 nm illumination in both anesthetized and awake mice with cranial windows (NA = 0.8; Linear FOV = 1 mm; focal depth = 250 μm) (Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: 1320 nm light experiences stronger water absorption and weaker scattering compared to 920 nm light.
source: In comparison, 1320 nm light experiences stronger water absorption and weaker scattering, which implies higher heat generation in a smaller volume, and therefore tissue temperature is expected to rise faster with input power (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated based on optical properties shown in Table 1.

claim: At 1 mm imaging depth, the maximum brain temperature starts to rise above 37 °C at 80 mW average power immediately after the objective lens with continuous scanning.
source: According to our simulation, at 1 mm imaging depth, the maximum brain temperature starts to rise above the normal body temperature of 37 °C at 80 mW average power immediately after the objective lens of 2 mm work distance (or 68 mW at the brain surface) with continuous scanning (Figure 3B and C; NA ~ 0.75; FOV = 230 μm).
evidence: This is calculated from Monte Carlo simulation shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: For power higher than 80 mW, the peak temperature rises at a rate of approximately 3 °C per 50 mW after the objective lens.
source: For power higher than 80 mW, the peak temperature rises at a rate of ~3 °C per 50 mW after the objective lens (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is calculated from Monte Carlo simulation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No tissue response was detected by measuring heat shock protein, microglial, or astrocytic activation at 100 mW average power in anesthetized mice.
source: According to the immunohistochemistry results, no tissue response was detected by measuring heat shock protein (﻿anti HSP-70/72), microglial (anti-GFAP), or astrocytic activation (﻿anti-Iba1) at 100 mW average power in anesthetized mice (NA = 0.75; Linear FOV = 230 µm; n = 5 mice, Figure 3—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is measured experimentally using immunohistochemistry.

claim: There is a non-zero chance (1 in 4 mice at 1 mm depth and 1 in 3 mice at 1.2 mm depth) of detectable tissue response with 150 mW imaging power.
source: however, there is a non-zero chance (1 in 4 mice at 1 mm depth and 1 in 3 mice at 1.2 mm depth) of detectable tissue response with 150 mW imaging power, based on visual inspection of the brain slices (Figure 3D) and the quantification of immunolabeling intensity (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is observed experimentally and shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: The immunohistochemistry results at 150 mW illumination suggest the upper bound of peak temperature should not exceed 41 °C.
source: Relating to the temperature calculation in Figure 3C, the immunohistochemistry results at 150 mW illumination suggest the upper bound of peak temperature should not exceed 41 °C, which is the peak temperature at an illumination power of 150 mW, according to our simulation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred by relating experimental results to simulation.

claim: The maximum brain temperature is lower with larger imaging depth for the same excitation power.
source: In general, the maximum brain temperature is lower with larger imaging depth or scanning FOV for the same excitation power.
evidence: This is stated as a general trend from simulations.

claim: The maximum brain temperature is lower with larger scanning FOV for the same excitation power.
source: In general, the maximum brain temperature is lower with larger imaging depth or scanning FOV for the same excitation power.
evidence: This is stated as a general trend from simulations.

claim: Brain heating is independent of the imaging frame rate when the temperature change between successive frames is negligible.
source: Brain heating is independent of the imaging frame rate when the temperature change between successive frames is negligible.
evidence: This is stated as a condition for modeling brain heating.

claim: Brain tissue cools at the rate of approximately 0.1 °C/s.
source: For example, because the brain tissue cools at the rate of ~0.1 °C/s (Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016), the temperature fluctuation at a given point in the tissue due to beam scanning is only ~0.05 °C at 2 Hz frame rate.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The water absorption coefficient at 1280 nm is approximately 65% of that at 1320 nm.
source: In addition to 1320 nm, we also simulated brain heating with 1280 nm excitation light since the water absorption coefficient at 1280 nm is ~65% of that at 1320 nm (Table 1), leading to less than 50% of the total photons absorbed in the illuminated volume (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated based on data in Table 1.

claim: 3PE with 1280 nm allows almost 50% more average power than 1320 nm with similar EAL.
source: As a result, 3PE with 1280 nm allows almost 50% more average power than 1320 nm with similar EAL (Kobat et al., 2009), which is potentially beneficial for maximizing imaging depth or FOV.
evidence: This is inferred from the lower water absorption and supported by a citation.

claim: Fluorescence saturation (ground-state depletion) of GCaMP6s occurs at 4-5 nJ under 3PE under the imaging conditions used.
source: For GCaMP6s, we calculated that fluorescence saturation (i.e., ground-state depletion) occurs at 4-5 nJ under 3PE under our imaging conditions (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is calculated based on the excitation probability equation.

claim: Laser-induced nonlinear damage can be observed in cells as a sudden but irreversible elevation to extraordinary brightness.
source: Laser-induced nonlinear damage can be observed in cells as a sudden but irreversible elevation to extraordinary brightness, which is caused by the rapid ionization and recombination of molecules followed by pressure increase (Tsai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The damage threshold for peak intensity increases with wavelength.
source: In general, the damage threshold for the peak intensity increases with wavelength (Fu et al., 2006; König et al., 1999; Olivié et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neurons remain healthy and viable for weeks after hours of exposure to 1.5 nJ pulses (60 fs and NA~0.75) at 1300-nm wavelength.
source: Our previous work showed that neurons remain healthy and viable for weeks after hours of exposure to 1.5 nJ pulses (60 fs and NA~0.75) at the 1300-nm wavelength (Ouzounov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Approximately 10 nJ at the focus causes tissue ablation.
source: As an estimate of the upper bound of pulse energy, we observed that ~10 nJ at the focus causes tissue ablation, in agreement with another independent study (Yildirim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is observed experimentally and supported by a citation.

claim: 1 to 2 nJ pulse energy at the focus (approximately 40 fs, NA approximately 1.0) does not appear to alter the physiological response of neurons under visual stimulation.
source: In addition, it was shown that 1 to 2 nJ pulse energy at the focus (~ 40 fs, NA ~ 1.0) does not appear to alter the physiological response of the neurons under visual stimulation (Yildirim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: 1 to 2 nJ pulse energy at the focus is reasonable for 3PM to achieve sufficient signal strength while avoiding nonlinear photodamage and fluorophore saturation.
source: Based on these results, 1 to 2 nJ pulse energy at the focus is reasonable for 3PM to achieve sufficient signal strength while avoiding nonlinear photodamage and fluorophore saturation.
evidence: This is concluded from the cited results and calculations.

claim: 1320 nm 3PM has the benefit of more efficient signal generation for calcium imaging in the deep mouse brain cortex compared to 920 nm 2PM.
source: In this study, we quantitatively compared 1320 nm 3PM and 920 nm 2PM for deep tissue GCaMP6 imaging. The 1320 nm 3PM has the benefit of more efficient signal generation and substantially higher SBR for calcium imaging in the deep mouse brain cortex.
evidence: This is concluded from the quantitative comparison.

claim: 1320 nm 3PM has substantially higher SBR for calcium imaging in the deep mouse brain cortex compared to 920 nm 2PM.
source: In this study, we quantitatively compared 1320 nm 3PM and 920 nm 2PM for deep tissue GCaMP6 imaging. The 1320 nm 3PM has the benefit of more efficient signal generation and substantially higher SBR for calcium imaging in the deep mouse brain cortex.
evidence: This is concluded from the quantitative comparison.

claim: 1320 nm 3PM outperforms 2PM in signal generation efficiency at a depth beyond approximately 700 μm in mouse neocortex regardless of labeling density.
source: We find that 1320 nm 3PM outperforms 2PM in signal generation efficiency at a depth beyond ~700 μm in mouse neocortex regardless of labeling density.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data.

claim: In the densely labeled mouse brain (CaMKII-GCaMP6s transgenic mouse), 1320 nm 3PM is preferred beyond the depth where SBR is approximately 1 (approximately 4 EALs or 600 μm in mice neocortex).
source: In the densely labeled mouse brain, for example CaMKII-GCaMP6s transgenic mouse, 1320 nm 3PM is preferred beyond the depth where SBR ~ 1 (e.g.,~4 EALs or 600 μm in mice neocortex).
evidence: This is concluded from the SBR measurements.

claim: Depending on labeling density and expression nonuniformity, 3PM might be considered at approximately 3 EALs or approximately 450 μm to prevent recording bias against neurons with lower expression levels.
source: In practice, depending on the labeling density and expression nonuniformity, 3PM might be considered at an even shallower depth to prevent recording bias against neurons with lower expression levels, for example ~3 EALs or ~450 μm (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is suggested based on the observation of dimmer neurons showing reduced ΔF/F in 2PM.

claim: Brain heating is significantly increased beyond 1350 nm due to water absorption.
source: Brain heating is significantly increased beyond 1350 nm due to water absorption (Jacques, 2013) and much reduced at 1280 nm (see the previous section).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and previous analysis.

claim: 1280 nm allows approximately 50% more average power than 1320 nm.
source: Even though 1280 nm allows ~ 50% more average power than 1320 nm, it only generates ~50% more signal since the signal scales linearly with the average power when the peak intensity is maximized and fixed.
evidence: This is stated based on the relationship between power and signal.

claim: The pulse energy at the focus should always be kept as high as possible (e.g., 1 to 2 nJ) to maximize the signal while avoiding adverse nonlinear effects.
source: Regardless of the imaging depth, the pulse energy at the focus should always be kept as high as possible (e.g., 1 to 2 nJ) to maximize the signal while avoiding the adverse nonlinear effects (e.g., fluorophore saturation and nonlinear damage).
evidence: This is stated as an optimization principle.

claim: The imaging power grows exponentially with depth.
source: The imaging power grows exponentially with depth, which is much faster than the quasi-linear growth of the heat dissipation capacity as a function imaging depth (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The maximum repetition rate decreases rapidly with imaging depth.
source: Therefore, the maximum repetition rate decreases rapidly with imaging depth.
evidence: This is inferred from the exponential growth of power with depth and thermal constraints.

claim: When imaging GCaMP6s-labeled neurons at 600 μm depth using 1320 nm 3PE, the maximum repetition rate to avoid substantial tissue temperature rise is 7 MHz.
source: For example, when imaging GCaMP6s-labeled neurons at 600 μm depth (~ 2 EALs) using 1320 nm 3PE, 1.86 nJ x exp(2) ~ 14 nJ pulse energy on the brain surface is required for 0.1 photon/pulse detected (Figure 1B), and the maximum repetition rate to avoid substantial tissue temperature rise is 100 mW/ 14 nJ = 7 MHz, where 100 mW is predicted as a safe power to avoid thermal damage at this imaging depth, given a large enough scanning FOV (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is calculated based on experimental data and simulations.

claim: When imaging the hippocampus at approximately 1 mm depth, the maximum repetition rate has to be reduced to 1.2 MHz.
source: When imaging the hippocampus at ~ 1 mm depth (~ 4 EALs due to the presence of the white matter), the maximum repetition rate has to be reduced to 120 mW/100 nJ = 1.2 MHz for the same signal generation level at the focus.
evidence: This is calculated based on experimental data and simulations.

claim: The pixel size is approximately the lateral spot size of the focus, for example two pixels per focal spot for proper spatial sampling frequency.
source: As a common practice, the pixel size is approximately the lateral spot size of the focus, for example two pixels per focal spot for a proper spatial sampling frequency.
evidence: This is stated as a common practice in imaging.

claim: Tissue heating is higher with a smaller FOV.
source: Tissue heating is higher with a smaller FOV, and therefore the imaging power should be reduced accordingly with the FOV (see Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: For calcium imaging, the frame rate should be fast enough for capturing the temporal dynamics of the calcium indicator (e.g., >5 Hz for GCaMP6s).
source: For calcium imaging, the frame rate should be fast enough for capturing the temporal dynamics of the calcium indicator (e.g.,>5 Hz for GCaMP6s).
